The AI Leadership Brief
Edition 08 · 9–15 Nov 2026 · By Jayaraman (Jay) Ganapathi, People Prime Worldwide · For CXOs and senior leaders
0 1 G R OW T H · P 1
CA R TO O N & TO P N E W S
↑ Agenda
Customer, or bot?
Yes.
Behind the cartoon: on 11 November an airline barred unauthorised third-party AI
agents from completing a purchase on its channels; on 13 November a leading AI
developer published what merchants must change before an agent can pay. An
agent is a customer and an automated visitor at the same time, and most checkout
defences were built to tell those two apart. Lead story, page 3 › · Skift ·

0 5 P E O P L E · P 1
L E A D E R S H I P AC T I O N S T H I S W E E K
↑ Agenda
1. Decide your agent policy explicitly. Name the executive who owns
whether AI agents may browse, buy and manage accounts on your
channels.
2. Find out what your site does today. Your firewall and bot rules already
answer this question, with no policy behind them.
3. Write down who you refund when an agent buys on a customer's behalf
and the order is disputed.
4. Inventory your partner and supplier portals against the FBI's list of entry
points, not just your main estate.
5. Check every AI line item against current list prices, including any that are
introductory and expire this month.
6. Ask whether your AI roadmap depends on one supplier's leadership,
and what your contract says about continuity.
7. If you operate in the EU, name who would own an AI Act sandbox
application ahead of the regulation's 1 December date of effect.
8. Ask HR for hours, age and education trends in your most exposed roles,
not just headcount.

employed, not how many. Its authors decline to call it cause and
effect. arXiv preprint

text:
W E E K LY · E D I T I O N 0 8
9 – 1 5 N OV 2 0 2 6 · PAG E 2 O F 7
The AI Leadership Brief
01 GROWTH · REGIONAL INDEX
0 1 G R OW T H · P 2
S E C TO R I N D E X · TO P 2 2 I N D U S T R I E S
↑ Agenda
Twenty-two sectors are swept each week against eight item types; all twenty-two carry an item this week, 9 of them tagged. A row tagged
UNQUALIFIED rests on trade or secondary reporting we could not trace to a first-party release or filing: it is published so the sector is covered, and
should be weighed as weaker than the rest of the issue.
SECTOR
THIS WEEK
SOURCE
01
Banking
Financial services, which covers banking, is named among the ten sectors targeted by the ARTEX framework in the
FBI's 13 Nov alert. Abu Dhabi Global Market's regulator issued a notice pairing AI governance with cyber risk.
FBI alert · ADGM
notice
02
Mortgage & lending
UNQUALIFIED
Dark Matter Technologies acquired the AI agent platform and intellectual property of House Numbers,
whose agents work loan conditions and contact borrowers, and named its co-founder chief AI officer. Terms were not
disclosed, and sources date the announcement variously to 30 Oct and the week of 13 Nov.
HousingWire · Natl
Mortgage Prof
03
Insurance
IBM and Microsoft announced Imagine Enterprise on 10 Nov, an agentic platform for building, running and governing
AI agents, launching with industry frameworks for financial services, insurance and retail. IBM Consulting contributes
more than 6,000 pre-built agents; Microsoft provides the AI, cloud and security technology.
IBM Newsroom
04
Capital markets & asset mgmt
The Ontario Securities Commission published findings from its examination of how registered firms use and govern AI,
including weaknesses in governance and training and instances of possible “AI washing”.
OSC release
05
Healthcare providers
Google Cloud launched Gemini for healthcare on 10 Nov in US preview, connecting electronic health records, billing
platforms, clinical guidelines and CMS datasets, with launch customers including HCA Healthcare, Northwell Health
and Optum. Separately, research among 182 operators reports 52.7% already running a live agentic workflow; it is
published by a firm that sells into the market it surveyed.
Google Cloud ·
Black Book
06
Pharma & life sciences
UNQUALIFIED
Pierre Fabre engaged XtalPi’s AI and robotics platform on 10 Nov to design small molecules for
undisclosed oncology targets, with Pierre Fabre taking any resulting candidates into the clinic.
World Pharma AI
07
Manufacturing & industrials
Agile Robots, a Munich physical-AI company whose robots automate industrial work, raised a $500M Series F on 12
Nov led by SoftBank, with NVIDIA, Hitachi and T.Capital named as participants. The company says its German plant
can build up to 10,000 legged and wheeled humanoid robots a year.
Agile Robots
announcement
08
Automotive & mobility
UNQUALIFIED
Executives at Nexperia and STMicroelectronics said on 10 Nov that chip capacity moving to AI data
centres and robotics is tightening supply of the mature-node components used in vehicles and industrial equipment,
pointing manufacturers towards longer procurement horizons. This is an AI-driven supply constraint, not an adoption
item.
Mfg briefing
09
Retail & e-commerce
OpenAI's wallet asks retailers not to block agents and to make risk systems recognise them, while one major travel
merchant went the other way. The IBM–Microsoft platform also covers retail.
OpenAI · IBM
10
Consumer goods
UNQUALIFIED
The president of Lowes Foods told a grocery conference, reported 10 Nov, that AI use among
shoppers is already widespread, citing a projection that 80% of shoppers will interact with AI by 2030 and putting the
2026 figure at 74%. Both are projections he cited, not his company’s data. Coty was separately reported piloting AI
discovery across six brands.
Consumer Goods
11
Energy & utilities
At the BNEF Houston Summit on 11 Nov a consultant advising the Utilize Coalition argued AI tools let grid planners see
capacity they could not see before. One adviser’s view, not a deployment; she also advises an AI data-centre
flexibility startup. Energy is named in the FBI’s targeted list.
Utility Dive · FBI
alert
12
Oil, gas & chemicals
UNQUALIFIED
Dated just before this window: on 3 Nov at ADIPEC, ADNOC agreed with G42 and OpenAI to become
the first energy company to deploy OpenAI Frontier, a platform for coordinating AI agents across operations.
WAM
13
Telecommunications
Telecommunications is named among the ten sectors the FBI says have been targeted by the ARTEX framework since
at least August 2026.
FBI alert
14
Media & entertainment
UNQUALIFIED
Disney and Adobe announced a multi-year partnership on 9 Nov to build generative AI models tailored
to Disney’s properties via Adobe’s Firefly Foundry, trained on character attributes, environments and visual styles to
produce what the companies call commercially safe output.
TheWrap
15
Technology & software
Nvidia reported a chief-executive transition in an 8-K filing. Technology is one of the ten sectors on the FBI's targeted
list.
NVIDIA 8-K · FBI
alert
16
Semiconductors & hardware
Fractile raised $720 million for inference chips integrating memory with logic, with UK state funds participating.
Semiconductors are also named in the FBI's targeted sector list.
SiliconANGLE · FBI
alert
17
Professional & legal services
Addleshaw Goddard said on 9 Nov it will distribute chatbot software from Harvey, a legal AI company, firmwide to
more than 3,400 lawyers and business services staff. Legal is also among the ten sectors in the FBI’s 13 Nov alert.
Law360 · FBI alert
18
Logistics & supply chain
UNQUALIFIED
DHL Supply Chain announced on 9 Nov the next phase of its digitalisation strategy, adding AI
orchestration to live warehouse operations to coordinate equipment, staff and workflows; it reports more than 9,000
robots across its network. GXO expanded a robotics partnership with Apptronik on 12 Nov.
Global Trade ·
Logistics
Viewpoints
19
Construction & real estate
UNQUALIFIED
A Federation of Master Builders and CIOB survey reported on 10 Nov found 57% of construction
businesses had increased AI use over 12 months, mostly for administration, with 33% using it in site operations, health
and safety or quality management. The FMB’s chief executive said technology alone would not solve the industry’s
wider challenges.
Sustainable
Construction
20
Agriculture & livestock
GEA showed DairyNet Intelligence at EuroTier on 11 Nov, an AI layer over its DairyNet herd management system
summarising a cow’s health from milk yield, activity, somatic cell count and conductivity. GEA says it is in testing, does
not yet recommend actions, and reaches selected farms in late 2026 or early 2027.
GEA trade press
release
21
Food & beverages
UNQUALIFIED
IFF launched CONCEPT MUSE, an AI platform that generates food and beverage concepts from
consumer insights, flavour expertise and market intelligence, producing product ideas and visual mock-ups. Its claim
to shorten early-stage development is the company’s own.
New Food
Magazine
22
Public sector, defence &
education
Government and defence are both named in the FBI alert. The EU set common rules for AI Act regulatory sandboxes;
the requirement on each member state to run one comes from the AI Act timeline, not this instrument.
FBI alert · EUR-Lex
The AI Leadership Brief · Edition 08
9–15 Nov 2026 · Page 2 of 7

W E E K LY · E D I T I O N 0 8
9 – 1 5 N OV 2 0 2 6 · PAG E 4 O F 7
The AI Leadership Brief
01 GROWTH · THE LEAD
0 1 G R OW T H · P 4
L E A D : T H E C H E C KO U T D E C I S I O N
↑ Agenda
AGENTIC COMMERCE · 11–13 NOV 2026 · UNITED STATES, GLOBAL
Within 48 hours, one airline locked unauthorised third-party AI agents out of its
checkout and OpenAI set out what merchants must change to accept agent payments
— a decision and a requirement, landing two days apart
On 11 November United Airlines said it would restrict “unauthorized, third-
party personal AI agents or assistants” from its website and app, and
indirectly through travel agencies and aggregators. The settled part is the
transaction: reports of its revised contract say an agent may not book, change
or service a ticket, or buy seats, upgrades or extras — and that this holds
even where the passenger supervises and approves every step. United has
said that a consumer granting an agent access does not by itself mean the
agent can transact. Accounts differ on whether searching and displaying fares
are also restricted: some report that search remains open, others that the
terms reach it, and we have not resolved it. Separately, its website terms
prohibit using its pricing, schedules and availability data to train or evaluate
machine learning models. United gave account security, unintended
transactions and regulatory concerns as its reasons.
On 13 November OpenAI launched ChatGPT Wallet, which lets agents
complete purchases with user approval, using tokenised cards. It was built
with American Express, Mastercard and Visa, and is limited at launch to
ChatGPT Pro subscribers in the United States aged 18 or over with eligible US-
issued cards. OpenAI says it does not hold customer funds. OpenAI also
published a playbook for merchants. It says that to accept payment from the
wallet, websites need to ensure agents are “not inadvertently blocked”, and
that payment and risk systems need to recognise legitimate purchases made
by agents. It points merchants at their CDN and firewall settings and at Web
Bot Auth, which lets an agent sign its requests.
Open: Skift on United, 11 Nov · CIO · PhocusWire, for United’s Digital Trust Center wording ·
OpenAI, 13 Nov · Digital Commerce 360 · Bloomberg
OUR SUMMARY · WHY THIS IS THE WEEK'S LEAD
Both point at one question: is an AI agent at the checkout a
customer or an intruder? Only the airline has answered it. OpenAI
has not — it has set out what a merchant must change in order to
answer yes, which is a condition of doing this business, not a
decision of its own.
Where a business has not taken this decision explicitly, it is being
settled anyway — by bot-detection rules, CDN settings and fraud
scoring configured before agents could buy anything. That is a
commercial policy set by default, by systems nobody briefed.
The unglamorous question underneath it is liability: when an agent
buys on a customer's behalf and the charge is disputed, who is
refunded, and on whose authority.
PARTY · DATE
POSITION ON AGENTS AT THE CHECKOUT
SOURCE
United Airlines
11 Nov · airline
Restricts unauthorised third-party personal AI agents across its own platforms and indirectly through agencies and
aggregators. An agent may not book, change or service a ticket, or buy extras, even where the passenger approves each
step. Accounts differ on whether display and search are also restricted. Terms bar use of its pricing and schedule data to
train or evaluate models.
Skift
OpenAI
13 Nov · model maker
Launched ChatGPT Wallet so agents can complete purchases with user approval, using tokenised cards and a security
check on every purchase. OpenAI says existing card protections are preserved and that it does not hold customer funds.
Its merchant playbook sets conditions for accepting these payments: sites must not inadvertently block agents, and risk
systems must recognise agent purchases.
OpenAI
Positions as described by each organisation or by the reports linked. Others in the same sector could not be placed: Southwest has made its flight inventory viewable to ChatGPT
users, and Expedia and Booking are reported to be working with OpenAI, but neither source says whether either lets an agent complete a purchase — the step that matters here.
Travel carries the clearest examples this week; the same question faces any business that sells through a website.
ONE MEASURED FINDING, WITH ITS CONFLICT STATED
In research reported by PhocusWire, two named agent products navigated 176 scripted booking requests as far as the payment step, with no captchas or
login walls stopping them. The requests included airline bookings but were not limited to them. The research is Propellic's, a travel marketing agency selling
services in the market it tested; the figure is its own and has not been independently replicated. Treat it as an indication that existing defences do not reliably
tell agents apart, not a measure of your own estate.
Open: PhocusWire
ASK YOUR LEADERSHIP TEAM · EDITOR'S QUESTIONS
 
The AI Leadership Brief · Edition 08
9–15 Nov 2026 · Page 4 of 7
If an AI agent tried to buy from us today, what would happen — and does
anyone here actually know?
▸
Who owns the decision: commercial, security, or whoever last configured the
bot rules?
▸
When an agent buys and the customer disputes the charge, who do we
refund, and what evidence do we have of authority?
▸
Are we losing orders right now from agents our defences silently turned away?
▸

S U P P L I E R & G OV E R N A N C E R I S K
↑ Agenda
CEO TRANSITION · 12 NOV 2026 · UNITED STATES
Nvidia's chief executive resigned and the CFO took the role on an interim basis —
the board's filing addresses the part buyers care about
In a filing dated 12 November, Nvidia said Jensen Huang had resigned as President, Chief Executive Officer and a board member, effective immediately.
Colette Kress, Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer, will serve as Interim Chief Executive Officer and continue as CFO until a permanent
successor is named. The board is searching for one and will consider internal and external candidates. Harvey C. Jones was appointed the company's
first-ever Chair of the Board. Kress has been CFO since September 2013, after nearly 25 years in finance roles at technology companies including Cisco
and Microsoft.
The filing gives no reason. It followed widely reported allegations about the former chief executive's personal conduct, which the filing does not address
and this brief does not report on. What the filing does address is continuity: the chair's statement speaks to operations, customer commitments and the
product roadmap, quoted below.
Open: NVIDIA Form 8-K, 12 Nov 2026 · CNN
OUR SUMMARY · WHAT A BUYER SHOULD TAKE FROM IT
A board that names continuity of customer commitments in its first statement is
telling you where it expects the questions to come from. For buyers the exposure
is not the person; it is concentration. If your AI roadmap assumes one supplier's
parts, prices and cadence, a leadership change there is a change to your plan.

The AI Leadership Brief
03 RISK
0 3 R I S K · P 6
L AW S , R U L E S & G U I DA N C E
↑ Agenda
Four regulators acted inside one week, in four different postures: the EU set operating rules, Abu Dhabi issued a supervisory notice, the United States
imposed licensing, and Ontario’s securities regulator published what an inspection had already found.
JURISDICTION ·
DATE
WHAT WAS ISSUED, AND WHAT IT REQUIRES
SOURCE
European Union
10–11 Nov
Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/2487, adopted 10 November and published in the Official Journal on 11
November, lays down common rules for the establishment, operation and supervision of the AI regulatory sandboxes
required by the AI Act. The Official Journal entry gives a date of effect of 1 December 2026 and records entry into force
as pending notification. The 2 August 2027 deadline for member states to run a national sandbox comes from the AI Act
timeline as amended, not from this instrument.
EUR-Lex, OJ L
2026/2487
UAE · ADGM
10 Nov
The Financial Services Regulatory Authority issued FCCP Notice No. 222 of 2026 on Artificial Intelligence and Cyber
Risk Management, pairing AI governance and cyber risk in a single supervisory instrument for firms in the financial free
zone. Our view: the structural choice is the notable part — the two are supervised together rather than separately.
FinReg-E
summary
Canada · Ontario
12 Nov
The Ontario Securities Commission published Staff Notice 33-763, setting out what its examination of registered firms
found about AI use and governance. It reports most firms early in adoption, with weaknesses in governance and training
and instances of possible “AI washing” — marketing claims about AI that firms could not substantiate. The OSC is a
provincial regulator; Canada has no single national securities regulator. Our view: findings from a completed
examination are a different thing from guidance — they show what a regulator actually found when it looked.
OSC release, 12
Nov
United States · BIS
15 Nov
The Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security issued an interim final rule extending export licensing
requirements to remote access to advanced AI chips in data centres outside the United States that supply large
amounts of compute to companies headquartered in certain jurisdictions, and formally rescinding the earlier AI Diffusion
Rule. Our view: the practical question for any business is whether compute it rents abroad now falls inside a licensing
requirement.
Law firm analysis
Qualification: the EU regulation is taken from the Official Journal text itself and the Ontario notice from the commission's own release. The ADGM notice is reported from a
regulatory summary rather than the regulator's own page, which we were unable to open for this issue; its date and instrument number are as that source gives them, so confirm
with the issuing regulator before acting. The US measure is an interim final rule, which takes effect while comment is still open, and is reported here only for its compliance effect.
0 3 R I S K · P 6
V E N D O R & S E C U R I T Y R I S K
↑ Agenda
FBI FLASH-20261113-001 · 13 NOV 2026 · TEN SECTORS
The FBI named ten sectors already targeted by an open-source AI intrusion framework, and
pointed at the systems companies watch least
On 13 November the FBI issued FLASH-20261113-001, “Threat Overview of
ARTEX Autonomous Penetration Testing Framework”. ARTEX is an open-
source, model-driven penetration-testing framework published on GitHub in
July 2026. The bureau says a variety of malicious actors have used it since at
least August 2026 to “automate multiple phases of cyber intrusions at
machine speed”, from reconnaissance through to data exfiltration.
The alert names ten targeted sectors: financial services, government,
technology, defence, semiconductors, energy, healthcare, manufacturing,
telecommunications and legal. It reports that some intrusions reached
privileged access in under three hours, and singles out partner and supplier
portals, mobile backends, sales-support systems, legacy services and third-
party integrations as the entry points it names. Incidents described in the
accounts linked below include attacks on financial institutions in South Korea
involving personal information of roughly 67,000 individuals, and a supply-
chain compromise affecting customers of a cloud backup product.
Open: Infosecurity Magazine (Kevin Poireault) · SecureWorld · SafeBreach. The FLASH itself
is distributed to recipients rather than published at a public URL; these are bylined accounts
of it. SafeBreach sells breach-simulation software and has a commercial interest in this
subject.
WHAT MAKES THIS A BOARD ITEM
The entry points the FBI names are not the systems most security
budgets defend. Partner portals, supplier integrations and sales-
support tools are typically owned by a business function, built by
someone else, and inventoried nowhere.
Our view: the three-hour figure changes the planning assumption
more than the framework does. A response process that assumes a
day or two of dwell time before privileged access is a process built
for a different attacker.
A separate count by Censys put publicly exposed ARTEX consoles
above 1,600 in early November. That is a count of exposed consoles,
not of breaches, and it is Censys's figure rather than the bureau's.

0 3 R I S K · P 6
V E N D O R & S E C U R I T Y R I S K
↑ Agenda

FBI FLASH-20261113-001 · 13 NOV 2026 · TEN SECTORS
The FBI named ten sectors already targeted by an open-source AI intrusion framework, and
pointed at the systems companies watch least
On 13 November the FBI issued FLASH-20261113-001, “Threat Overview of

ARTEX Autonomous Penetration Testing Framework”. ARTEX is an open-
source, model-driven penetration-testing framework published on GitHub in
July 2026. The bureau says a variety of malicious actors have used it since at
least August 2026 to “automate multiple phases of cyber intrusions at
machine speed”, from reconnaissance through to data exfiltration.

The alert names ten targeted sectors: financial services, government,
technology, defence, semiconductors, energy, healthcare, manufacturing,
telecommunications and legal. It reports that some intrusions reached

privileged access in under three hours, and singles out partner and supplier
portals, mobile backends, sales-support systems, legacy services and third-
party integrations as the entry points it names. Incidents described in the
accounts linked below include attacks on financial institutions in South Korea
involving personal information of roughly 67,000 individuals, and a supply-
chain compromise affecting customers of a cloud backup product.

Open: Infosecurity Magazine (Kevin Poireault) · SecureWorld · SafeBreach. The FLASH itself
is distributed to recipients rather than published at a public URL; these are bylined accounts
of it. SafeBreach sells breach-simulation software and has a commercial interest in this
subject.
WHAT MAKES THIS A BOARD ITEM

The entry points the FBI names are not the systems most security
budgets defend. Partner portals, supplier integrations and sales-

support tools are typically owned by a business function, built by
someone else, and inventoried nowhere.
Our view: the three-hour figure changes the planning assumption

more than the framework does. A response process that assumes a
day or two of dwell time before privileged access is a process built
for a different attacker.

A separate count by Censys put publicly exposed ARTEX consoles
above 1,600 in early November. That is a count of exposed consoles,
not of breaches, and it is Censys's figure rather than the bureau's.

0 5 P E O P L E · P 7
WO R K F O R C E & TA L E N T · R E S E A R C H
↑ Agenda
A labour-market preprint finds the early effects of
AI in who is working, not how many are working
A revised preprint posted to arXiv on 10 November examines how labour
outcomes have changed across occupations as AI capability advanced from
chatbots to reasoning models and agents. The authors build an occupational
AI exposure score from task-level assessments against O*NET task data and
link it to US Current Population Survey records. In the revised version, part-
time work declined, weekly hours rose slightly, and the workforce in exposed
occupations became older and more educated — effects appearing in the
composition of the workforce rather than in the number of jobs.
The authors' own caveats do most of the work here. They state that they
“refrain from interpreting the estimated coefficients as causal effects”. They
warn that standard errors are likely understated, because the public-use
survey lacks the identifiers needed for design-based corrections, and advise
weighting magnitude and direction over statistical significance. The exposure
score measures potential capability, not actual adoption or substitution. They
name post-pandemic recovery, interest rates and trade policy as possible
confounders.
Open: arXiv:2507.08244 — Jacob Dominski and Yong Suk Lee, University of Notre Dame,
econ.GN. Preprint, not peer reviewed. Version note: arXiv's own rendered copies carry a v3
stamp dated 10 Nov 2026 and the findings above, while the listing page we retrieved shows
only v1 from July 2025, whose reported results differ — an earlier version associated higher
exposure with reduced employment. We report the revised version and flag the discrepancy
rather than resolving it.
OUR SUMMARY · WHY A CHRO SHOULD CARE
Most workforce planning for AI is expressed as a headcount number.
If the early effects really do land in composition — hours, age mix,
education mix, full-time share — then a headcount forecast can look
stable while the shape of the workforce underneath it changes
considerably.
That is a measurement question you can answer in your own data
this quarter, without waiting for the literature to settle: it is the one
claim here you do not have to take on trust.
Given the caveats above, treat this as a hypothesis worth testing
internally, not a finding to plan on.

Siemens Energy reported record quarterly revenue this week, with its chief executive saying he has “no doubt” more data centres will be built in the
United States, while noting that gas remains the main driver of generation. Our view: for most businesses this is a cost and siting line rather than a
sustainability one — power availability is becoming a constraint on where compute can be bought, and therefore on what it costs. A US federal electricity
forecast attributing record consumption partly to AI data centres was also reported this week. Its figures are held back until they can be cited to the
agency's own publication.
